subject: physics
title: National and global energy resources
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: National and global energy resources — AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification, section 4.1.3.
meta_desc: GCSE Physics (AQA) practice covering National and global energy resources, specification section 4.1.3.
final_note: You worked through National and global energy resources — 14 specification statements.

concepts.def: A supply of energy available for people to use. The main energy resources available for use on Earth include fossil fuels (coal, oil and gas), nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves. Electricity is not itself an energy resource: it has to be generated using one of these resources.

Fuels formed underground from the remains of living organisms over many millions of years. They are non-renewable: new fossil fuel forms far more slowly than the fuel is being used, so the supply is not replenished as it is used.

Fuel such as uranium, mined from rock and used in nuclear power stations. It is non-renewable, because the supply in the ground is finite and is not replenished as it is used. It releases no carbon dioxide while generating, but it produces radioactive waste.

Fuel made from plant or animal material grown recently, for example wood, or ethanol and biodiesel made from crops. It is renewable, because the crops used to make it can be grown again as the fuel is used. It is burned, so it releases carbon dioxide.

A renewable resource that uses the energy of moving air, mainly to generate electricity. Wind speed changes with the weather, so the output cannot be guaranteed at any particular moment: wind is not a reliable resource.

A renewable resource that uses water held behind a dam, usually in a river valley, to generate electricity. It is replenished by rainfall, and output can normally be supplied when it is wanted, but building the dam floods land.

A renewable resource that uses energy from hot rock beneath the Earth's surface, both for heating and for generating electricity. The rock stays hot day and night in all weathers, so geothermal is reliable, but it is only available in suitable places.

A renewable resource that uses the regular rise and fall of the sea. The tidal cycle repeats predictably each day and does not depend on the weather, so the tides are a reliable resource, although tidal schemes can alter coastal habitats.

A renewable resource. Sunlight is used to generate electricity and also to heat water directly. The energy arriving varies with the time of day, the season and the cloud cover, so the Sun is not a reliable resource on its own.

A renewable resource that uses the movement of waves on the surface of the sea. Wave size depends on the wind, so like wind itself this resource is not reliable. It is a different resource from hydro-electricity and from the tides.
An energy resource that is being (or can be) replenished as it is used. The renewable resources are bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves.
An energy resource that is not replenished as it is used, so the amount available falls as it is used up. The non-renewable resources are the fossil fuels - coal, oil and gas - and nuclear fuel.

Moving people and goods. Most transport runs on fuels refined from oil - petrol, diesel and aviation fuel. Bio-fuel is used in some vehicles, nuclear fuel powers some ships and submarines, and electricity is used in electric vehicles and trains.

Producing electricity for homes and industry. Almost every resource can be used for this: fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, bio-fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves. How each resource is used to generate the electricity is not required.
Warming buildings and water. This is done mainly by burning gas, oil or wood (a bio-fuel), and in some places by using geothermal energy, by solar heating of water, or by electricity.

A reliable energy resource is one that can supply energy whenever it is needed. Fossil fuels, nuclear fuel and bio-fuel can be burned on demand; geothermal is always available and the tides follow a predictable cycle, so these are reliable. Wind, the Sun and water waves depend on conditions that change from hour to hour, and hydro-electricity depends on rainfall, so these are less reliable.

The harm done to the environment by obtaining and using an energy resource. Every resource has some impact: renewable does not mean harmless. Impacts include gases released into the atmosphere, waste that must be stored, land taken or flooded, habitats damaged, and noise and visual intrusion.

concepts.term: Carbon dioxide released by burning fuels
concepts.def: Burning fossil fuels and bio-fuels releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere. Increasing the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere contributes to global warming and climate change. Nuclear fuel, wind, hydro-electricity, geothermal, the tides, the Sun and water waves do not release carbon dioxide as they are used.

Coal and oil contain sulfur impurities. When they are burned, sulfur dioxide is released, and this contributes to acid rain, which damages trees, soils, lakes and buildings. Carbon dioxide does not cause acid rain.

Using nuclear fuel produces waste that remains radioactive and dangerous for a very long time, so it must be stored securely. There is also the risk, however small, of an accident releasing radioactive material.

concepts.term: Impact on land, habitats and views
concepts.def: Renewable schemes take up space and change places. Hydro-electric dams flood valleys and destroy habitats, tidal schemes alter estuaries and the wildlife living there, wind farms are noisy and are objected to as a spoiling of the view, and growing crops for bio-fuel uses land that could grow food and can clear natural habitat.

concepts.term: Patterns and trends in the use of energy resources
concepts.def: Over recent decades the share of energy supplied by renewable resources has grown and the share supplied by coal has fallen, driven by concern about climate change, by government targets and by the falling cost of renewable schemes. Change is slow because new schemes are expensive and take years to build, because existing vehicles, boilers and power stations were built for fossil fuels, and because some renewables are less reliable.

concepts.term: Political, social, ethical and economic considerations
concepts.def: Science can identify an environmental issue caused by using an energy resource, but it does not by itself have the power to deal with it. What is actually done depends on political decisions, on what people are willing to accept, on ethical judgements about fairness to other countries and to future generations, and on the economic cost of change and the jobs and industries involved.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly classifies nuclear fuel and gives the correct reason?
options: Renewable, because generating with it does not release any carbon dioxide
Non-renewable, because nuclear fuel is one of the fossil fuels found in rock
Renewable, because a small mass of fuel lasts for a very long time indeed
Non-renewable, because the uranium used is not replenished as it is used
mcqs.explain: Classification follows the specification's test: a renewable resource is one being, or able to be, replenished as it is used. Uranium in the ground is not, so nuclear fuel is non-renewable.

mcqs.q: Which group contains only renewable energy resources?
options: Bio-fuel, geothermal and water waves
Nuclear fuel, geothermal and the tides
Bio-fuel, water waves and natural gas
Coal, bio-fuel and hydro-electricity
mcqs.explain: All three are replenished as they are used: crops are regrown, the rock stays hot, and waves keep forming.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the correct definition of a renewable energy resource?
options: One that will never run out, however quickly it is used up
One that gives out no carbon dioxide at all when it is used
One that is being, or can be, replenished as it is used
One that supplies energy at a steady rate whenever needed
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's definition exactly: replenishment keeping pace with use.

mcqs.q: Why is bio-fuel classified as a renewable energy resource?
options: Because burning bio-fuel causes no environmental damage at all
Because burning bio-fuel releases no carbon dioxide into the air
Because the plants used to make it are grown again as it is used
Because the world's supply of bio-fuel can never be used up
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's test applied directly: the resource is replenished as it is used.

mcqs.q: New coal is still forming underground today. Why is coal still classed as non-renewable?
options: Non-renewable resources are the ones that give off polluting gases
It forms far more slowly than it is used, so it is not replenished
Non-renewable resources are the ones that supply energy reliably
It is being replenished, so it should really be classed as renewable
mcqs.explain: The test is whether replacement keeps pace with use. Coal forms over millions of years and is burned in decades.

mcqs.q: Which one of these energy resources is non-renewable?
options: Hydro-electricity, using water held behind a dam
Bio-fuel, made from crops that are grown for burning
Geothermal, using heat from rock under the surface
Nuclear fuel, from uranium that is mined from rock
mcqs.explain: The uranium in the ground is finite and is not replenished as it is used, so nuclear fuel is non-renewable.

mcqs.q: Which energy resource supplies most of the energy used for transport worldwide?
options: Oil, which is refined into petrol, diesel and aviation fuel
Coal, which is burned in the engines of most road vehicles
Electricity, because all vehicles now run on rechargeable batteries
Natural gas, which is piped straight to filling stations for cars
mcqs.explain: Transport runs overwhelmingly on fuels refined from oil, which is why transport is the hardest use to move away from fossil fuels.

mcqs.q: A house is heated by burning natural gas in a boiler. Which statement about this is correct?
options: Gas is only ever used to generate electricity, never for heating
Gas is a non-renewable fossil fuel, used here for heating
Gas is renewable, because new gas keeps forming under the sea
Gas is renewable, because it burns more cleanly than coal does
mcqs.explain: Correctly names the resource type and the use. Heating is a use of energy resources in its own right, separate from generation.

mcqs.q: Which resource can be used for all three of transport, electricity generation and heating?
options: Water waves, which can drive vehicles as well as power stations
Bio-fuel, which is burned in vehicles, power stations and boilers
Geothermal, which is used in vehicles and in power stations
The tides, which are used in vehicles and to heat buildings
mcqs.explain: Bio-fuel serves all three named uses: it drives vehicles, generates electricity and heats buildings when burned as wood.

mcqs.q: Solar panels on a roof warm water for a house. Which use of energy resources is this?
options: Electricity generation, since solar panels always make electricity
Electricity generation, since the hot water later drives a turbine
Neither, because sunlight in the UK is far too weak to heat water
Heating, because energy from the Sun warms the water directly
mcqs.explain: The Sun is being used for heating, one of the three named uses; no electricity is produced at any stage.

mcqs.q: Why is a wind farm a less reliable energy resource than a gas-fired power station?
options: Wind turbines break down far more often than a gas power station
Each turbine transfers much less energy than a gas power station
The wind does not always blow, so output cannot be guaranteed
Wind farms do more damage to the environment than gas stations
mcqs.explain: Reliability means energy is available when it is wanted. Wind speed varies with the weather, so it cannot be guaranteed.

mcqs.q: Tidal energy is described as a reliable resource. Which statement explains why?
options: The tides transfer far more energy than any other resource
Tidal equipment is stronger, so it hardly ever breaks down
The tides depend on the weather, which is easy to forecast
The tides rise and fall in a regular, predictable daily cycle
mcqs.explain: Because the cycle repeats predictably and does not depend on the weather, the supply can be counted on in advance.

mcqs.q: A country needs electricity at all hours, in any weather. Which resources suit that best?
options: Nuclear fuel and gas, because their output can be controlled
Wind and water waves, because there is always some wind
Solar only, because sunlight reaches the ground each day
Solar and wind, because renewables are the best resources
mcqs.explain: Both can supply energy on demand whatever the weather, which is exactly what reliability means.

mcqs.q: Which environmental impact arises mainly from burning fossil fuels?
options: Carbon dioxide released into the atmosphere as the fuel burns
Radioactive waste that has to be stored safely for many years
Loss of habitat when a river valley is flooded behind a dam
No impact at all, provided that the fuel is burned efficiently
mcqs.explain: Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide, and the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide contributes to climate change.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an environmental impact of burning coal in a power station?
options: Release of radioactive waste that must be stored for years
Release of carbon dioxide, which then falls as acid rain
No impact, because coal is a natural material from the ground
Release of sulfur dioxide, which contributes to acid rain
mcqs.explain: Coal contains sulfur impurities, so burning it releases sulfur dioxide, and this contributes to acid rain.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the environmental impact of renewable resources is correct?
options: Renewable resources have no environmental impact of any kind
Growing crops for bio-fuel has no effect on land or wildlife
Hydro-electric schemes can flood valleys and destroy habitats
Using wind uses the wind up, so there will be less wind later
mcqs.explain: Damming a valley covers land with water, which destroys the habitats there. Renewable does not mean harmless.

mcqs.q: Which environmental impact is associated with the use of nuclear fuel?
options: Large amounts of carbon dioxide released while generating
Sulfur dioxide released, which then causes acid rain to form
Radioactive waste that stays dangerous for a very long time
None, because nuclear fuel is a very concentrated energy source
mcqs.explain: This is the characteristic impact of nuclear fuel: waste that remains radioactive and must be stored securely.

mcqs.q: The share of UK electricity generated from renewables has risen sharply. Why?
options: Concern about climate change has driven investment in renewables
Renewable schemes have always been the cheapest option there is
Fossil fuels ran out completely, so nothing else was left to use
Renewable resources became reliable enough to be used on their own
mcqs.explain: The environmental impact of burning fossil fuels, together with government targets and falling costs, explains the trend.

mcqs.q: Fossil fuels still supply much of the world's energy. Why is the change away so slow?
options: Renewable resources have already replaced them almost everywhere
Building new schemes costs a great deal and takes many years
Scientists do not agree that fossil fuels harm the environment
Fossil fuels are renewable, so there is no reason to change now
mcqs.explain: Economic cost, the time to build, and equipment already designed for fossil fuels all slow the change down.

mcqs.q: Scientists identified the harm caused by burning fossil fuels, yet their use goes on. Why?
options: Science can always solve a problem once it has identified it
Political, social, ethical and economic factors limit what is done
The evidence for the harm is not accepted by most scientists
Governments have in fact already stopped all fossil fuel use
mcqs.explain: This is the specification's point: science identifies the issue but these considerations govern what is actually done.
